arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Stevenson argued Sullivan was 13 at arrest. He stated Sullivan was convicted of sexual assault. He noted the sentence was life without parole.
Mr. Makar argued the data supporting Sullivan is unreliable. He contrasted this with the rich literature in death penalty cases.
Justice Scalia questioned the applicability of Roper to this case. He noted Roper involved a death penalty context.
Justice Ginsburg raised the two-year statute of limitations. She noted the petition was filed in 2007. She asked if correcting a sentence overtakes the limitation.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Sullivan was 13 when convicted of sexual assault. He received a life sentence without parole. Florida law sets a two-year limit for post-conviction claims. Sullivan filed his claim in 2007. The conviction occurred in 1993. The state argues the time limit applies. Sullivan argues the limit blocks federal rights.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Sullivan wants the Court to strike down the state time limit. He argues the limit blocks his federal constitutional claim.
Florida wants the Court to uphold the state time limit. It argues the limit bars Sullivan's late claim.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Sullivan argues the state time limit violates federal law. He claims the limit prevents him from challenging his sentence.
Florida argues the state time limit is valid. It claims the limit bars Sullivan's late claim.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if Roper applies to non-death cases. He questioned the relevance of death penalty precedents here.
Justice Alito asked if the state judge decided Roper required the result. He sought clarity on the independent state ground argument.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines when states can block federal claims. It affects all juveniles facing life sentences. It clarifies the power of state time limits. It shapes the balance between state and federal law.
